Key success criteria are p50/p95 latency within SLA, throughput matching 80% of production peak during sustained window, deterministic quality regression under 5% misclassification for reranking flows, and reproducible telemetry for cost modeling.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-21 15:00 UTC; Duration: ~62 mins; Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel (CSM), Mark (Coriant Eng), Tanya (PM), Omar (Infra), Jules (DS)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time—quick intro, I'm Alex, AE on the account. Priya and Daniel from our side. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Mark (Coriant): Good, thanks. We wanted to scope a POC that mirrors a pretty complex production mix.
[00:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Great. We got your notes, Tanya, about needing both streaming chat-like calls and bulk non-streaming rerank jobs. Today we want to lock success criteria, what scripts you'll hand us, and the harness approach.
[00:30] Tanya: Yes, we have three core flows. One is interactive support chat (short context, streaming), second is a nightly rerank for search (non-streaming, batch), and third is a hybrid enrichment pipeline where we kick off long context summaries.
[00:46] Jules (Coriant DS): And we have fringe cases—like very long system prompts and some tokenization oddities.
[00:52] Omar: Network wise, we need VPC peering for the private POC, and we have a firewall restriction that blocks outbound ephemeral ports—so keep that in mind.
[01:05] Priya: Noted. We'll need the exact CIDR and egress rules. For the harness, our typical pattern is an adapter that takes your customer scripts and maps to our streaming SDK or REST generator.
[01:18] Mark: Quick question, what's the best way to keep script fidelity? We can't sanitise too much because that changes model behavior.
[01:25] Priya: We usually do a templating layer—variables for user fields but keep prompt structure intact. For fuzzing we can inject slight variations to simulate real world noise—typos, different length contexts.
[01:38] Alex: On success metrics—what matters to you? Latency SLO, throughput, cost, quality?
[01:45] Tanya: All of the above. Primary is latency p95 under 350ms for interactive flows at our 95th percentile QPS. Secondary is rerank throughput: we want to be able to process our nightly job within a 2-hour window. Quality loss for switching quantized models should be under 5% measured by our existing rerank metric.
[02:03] Jules: Also want deterministic logs and token-level timing so we can map cost.
[02:08] Priya: Good. We'll produce token-level timing, per-request cost estimate, and a workload heatmap.
[02:14] [Alex]: For the POC shape, are you leaning hosted vs dedicated vs private for the test infra?
[02:20] Mark: Private. We need to test with our internal data patterns and peering. But we might want a hosted baseline quick run first for debugging.
[02:29] Priya: Makes sense. We'll do a small hosted smoke and then the private run with VPC peering.
[02:36] Omar: About streaming—our client SDK uses incremental partial results for UI, we need sub-100ms token emission ideally. Is that realistic?
[02:46] Priya: Sub-100ms token emission consistently is challenging across long contexts; we can usually get low per-token latency with warm KV cache and persistent sessions. Cold-start tail latency will be higher—do you have cold-start patterns?
[02:59] Mark: Yes, we see cold spikes when a user hits after 30+ minutes of idle.
[03:05] Priya: Then we should include cold-start mix in the harness. We can model steady-state and cold-start windows.
[03:12] [00:03:20] Alex: Let's talk numbers—what QPS are we trying to emulate?
[03:17] Tanya: Peak interactive 120 RPS sustained for 10 minutes, average 40 RPS. Rerank batch is 50k items per hour.
[03:26] Priya: Perfect. For the harness we'll design two parallel jobs: streaming generator to hit 120 RPS with the exact message sequences, and a batch runner to submit rerank jobs at the nightly cadence. We'll also do traffic mirroring where feasible.
[03:41] Mark: Traffic mirroring—can you talk through how you mirror without impacting prod? We can't forward real PII to an external service.
[03:49] Priya: Right. We recommend local mirroring into an internal staging queue first and then a masked subset is sent to the POC environment. Our adapter supports field-level redaction rules; you provide the regexes or our default masks PII heuristically.
[04:03] Jules: Heuristic masking sometimes breaks structured prompts. We'll share exact fields.
[04:09] Priya: Good. We'll run a dry run on 10% of traffic, then ramp. For script fidelity, we will not change prompt tokens except variable substitution unless you ask us to.
[04:20] [00:04:30] Alex: On tooling—we will share a sample harness adapter repo (link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/harness-adapters/sample-adapter) and a README. That repo includes streaming and non-streaming examples.
[04:33] Mark: Awesome. If we use your adapter, how intrusive is it to our stack? Does it need agent installs?
[04:39] Priya: No agents—it's a lightweight shim that runs where you run your traffic mirroring agent. For private POC we'll set up a peered network path and an adapter container.
[04:49] Omar: About perf counters—what metrics do you surface?
[04:53] Priya: Token RT, model server CPU/GPU utilization, concurrency per worker, latency p50/p95, memory/KV cache hit rates, batching efficiency, and tokenization outs. Also per-request cost estimate.
[05:08] Tanya: We'll need an exportable CSV for our finance team.
[05:11] Priya: Yes, CSV & dashboard link.
[05:15] [00:05:30] Mark: Let's dig into streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs—if we convert some of our interactive flows to non-streaming to reduce per-token overhead, will we save cost?
[05:25] Priya: Potentially. Streaming keeps latency low for perceived responsiveness but can reduce batching efficiency. Non-streaming (micro-batching) can increase throughput at lower cost but hurts UX. We can show tradeoff curves using your scripts.
[05:37] Jules: For rerank we definitely want non-streaming. For chat maybe hybrid where we buffer short 50–100ms windows.
[05:45] Priya: That's exactly the mixed-mode we can simulate—streaming with intermittent micro-batch windows. We'll instrument the cost per effective token.
[05:53] [00:06:00] Alex: On quantization—you mentioned keeping quality within 5%. Do you have a preferred model family?
[06:00] Mark: We're starting with an Llama-derivative open model. We want a quantized 4-bit variant if possible to reduce GPU footprint.
[06:08] Priya: We support q4f and q3 variants. We'll run quality A/B on your rerank metric and provide diffs. Expect some small drift; we'll flag any regression >5% as a fail.
[06:19] Omar: How do you handle KV cache correctness for long context? We've seen cache evictions cause hallucinations.
[06:25] Priya: We'll configure cache TTLs and partition sizes; also include long-context tests in the fuzz suite to detect eviction-induced regressions.
[06:33] [00:06:40] Alex: Timeline—how long for us to run an end-to-end POC with benchmark runs and reporting?
[06:38] Priya: Typical is 3 weeks: week 1 onboarding + adapter integration, week 2 smoke testing and small benchmarks, week 3 full runs and analysis. We can compress to 2 weeks if both sides are ready and provide scripts early.
[06:51] Tanya: We're aiming for a two-week window because of stakeholder availability.
[06:54] Alex: So milestone plan: Day 0–3 infra + peering and adaptor, Day 4–7 sample smoke, Day 8–12 full benchmark runs, Day 13–14 analysis and report.
[07:06] Mark: Sounds good. Who owns the benchmarks? Are they run by Redwood SE?
[07:11] Priya: Redwood SE runs them in partnership with your infra team. We'll need to coordinate the exact time windows to ensure no resource contention.
[07:19] Jules: For acceptance, besides latency and throughput, we need reproducible cost estimates for billing.
[07:25] Daniel (CSM): We will include a cost model spreadsheet with per-token, per-hour GPU costs and an expected monthlyized cost.
[07:32] [00:07:40] Mark: Security—SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration are must-haves.
[07:38] Alex: We'll share SOC2 summary, SAML guide, and KMS patterns. Daniel will attach the SOC2 and security whitepaper.
[07:45] Omar: For VPC peering we need IP allowlist and our infra contact. We'll send owner details.
[07:51] Priya: Also note we can do a data flow diagram for your audit team.
[07:55] [00:08:00] Tanya: About validation—we want automated regression tests that run on any model swap and produce a pass/fail.
[08:05] Priya: We'll plug your evals into our optimize suite; we can configure per-prompt tolerance and regression alerting. The harness will run those tests at the end of each benchmark run.
[08:15] Mark: Regarding the harness adapter, is there a standard mapping for our internal message schema?
[08:20] Priya: Yes, the adapter accepts a mapping YAML where you declare roles, fields that map to system/user/assistant, and tokenization hints. We'll give you a template.
[08:30] [00:08:40] Alex: Any blockers we need to call out?
[08:34] Omar: Firewall egress, and timing windows for running the nightly rerank—we need to ensure it doesn't collide with backups.
[08:40] Mark: Also test data anonymization rules; we'll finalize which fields are PII.
[08:44] Priya: Ok we'll proceed with a 10% masked mirror first. If that looks good we ramp.
[08:51] Daniel: I'll send calendar invites for the dry run and the full run.
[08:55] Alex: Quick recap and next steps: Redwood to share adapter repo and security docs by Friday (2026-10-23), customer to share scripts and network details by 2026-10-28, schedule dry run on 2026-11-02. Anything else?
[09:10] Tanya: Please include a checklist for success criteria in the deliverables.
[09:14] Priya: Will do.
[09:16] Mark: Thanks all.
[09:18] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links.

End of transcript. Some ASR notes: 'KV' was sometimes transcribed as 'kay vee', 'VPC' as 'vee pee see' and occasional missing punctuation. There's mild crosstalk during the timeline planning (overlap at ~00:06:50).
